continuity-g7bty0.name: Continuity
continuity-g7bty0.summary: Wiki facts rot silently: nobody edited the page, the world just moved. Continuity re-checks each fact against the live web and drafts the fix for a maintainer to approve.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They assumed the expensive step (generation, review, data entry) should be priced before it runs.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: Wiki facts rot silently: nobody edited the page, the world just moved. Continuity re-checks each fact against the live web and drafts the fix for a maintainer to approve.
steal_this: Invert the pipeline: generate last, verify first. Ship the checker as the artifact and the content as its output.
Anything the architecture can enforce, the architecture enforces. Probabilistic components get proposals; deterministic components get verdicts.
Find the metric practitioners already eyeball, instrument it, and ship the delta. A number turns a vibe into a product.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then Continuity made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any tool with an expensive generation step

audit.worth_note: The diagnosis is worth more than the demo: a fact that used to be true and quietly stopped being true looks exactly like every correct sentence around it, and nobody edited the page — the world moved on. Treating wiki rot as a decay problem with a per-claim due date instead of an error problem is the right shape, and keeping the human as writer of record (a cited diff, never a publish) is the right posture for public knowledge infrastructure. The write-up also documents its own development discipline in the same breath as the product, which lets a reader check the cost claim against the fixture claim.

assumptions: a wiki or knowledge base with a review workflow you can post diffs into (MediaWiki pending changes, or a PR-style flow)
a per-claim research budget, since a pass costs a search plus several model calls for every claim on the page
a decision about contested facts: staff the disagreement bucket, or suppress that category rather than flood maintainers
clone_cost.estimate: 2-3 weeks — the ledger is the project, the model calls are glue
clone_cost.why: The walkthrough is ordinary orchestration over two APIs: extract, prioritise, research, judge, draft, cross-check, render a diff. What takes the time is the claim ledger — extracting claims reliably, keying them so a re-run recognises the same claim in a re-edited article, and the due-date and link graph on top — plus the fixture recorder that keeps iteration cheap. The dependency-free core design is what makes the second part cheap to get right.

audit.what_to_steal: Record fixtures on the first live run — write every search result and model response to disk once, and every later iteration is free; that single habit is what made the whole thing developable on a hackathon budget. Keep vendor SDKs at the edges around a dependency-free core so the interesting logic runs on a bare interpreter with no key. Schedule re-verification per claim with a last-checked and next-due time rather than per page, and keep a link graph between claims so an edit to one paragraph can be checked against its neighbours. And always hand back a diff with citations instead of writing to the system of record.
audit.what_breaks_first: The fixed staleness window. 'Skip what was verified last week' is a single guess about decay rates applied uniformly, and it is wrong in both directions for the facts this targets: a film's release date almost never moves, while 'current holder of X' can move in a day — so the budget is spent re-checking stable facts while the volatile ones age out between passes. Second: the reviewer's queue. 'Sources disagree' is a terminal category with no triage described, and on a long contested article it can hold a large share of the claims; a maintainer handed forty cited diffs and thirty unresolved disagreements has been given a new job, not a lighter one.

prior_art.relation: the same shape — a machine ranking facts for a human to act on, deliberately stopping short of acting — and the two pages differ almost entirely on whether the judgement is checkable: Continuity returns old text, new text, a citation and a confidence score per claim, while the fisheries tool returns a risk classification whose own page says there is no ground truth for it.

both convert an unverifiable judgement into an artifact a person can check (a cited diff, a signed finding) and both keep the human as the writer of record; the difference is what they attach evidence to — one grounds a claim against the live web on a schedule, the other against a versioned rule set in CI.

both are staged agent pipelines that publish a dollar figure, and read together they move the number worth tracking: Greenlight quotes cost per run against a measured output, Continuity quotes total build cost and explains that fixtures made every later iteration free — so iteration cost, not run cost, is what decides whether a pipeline is developable.
